chapter_summary:
The Screen and Output modules are the graphics and text output components of the Jack OS. They provide high-level functions for drawing on the screen, abstracting the low-level memory-mapped I/O that we explored in Module 3.

**Screen module:**

The Screen module provides functions for drawing graphics on the Hack screen. The screen is 256 rows by 512 columns of pixels, each pixel being black (1) or white (0). The screen is memory-mapped to addresses 16384 to 24575.

**Screen memory organization:**
- The screen is divided into 256 rows.
- Each row has 512 pixels, stored as 32 words of 16 bits each.
- The address of a word at row r, word w is: `16384 + r * 32 + w`.
- The bit position of pixel c within a word is: `c % 16`.

**Drawing a pixel:**
```jack
Screen.drawPixel(x, y):
    // Compute word address: 16384 + y * 32 + x / 16
    // Compute bit mask: 1 << (x % 16)
    // Read current word, OR with mask (for black) or AND with ~mask (for white), write back
```

**Drawing a line (Bresenham's algorithm):**

The Screen module uses a simple line drawing algorithm. For a line from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2):
1. Calculate the slope: `dy = y2 - y1`, `dx = x2 - x1`.
2. Iterate along the x-axis (or y-axis for steep lines), computing the corresponding y (or x) value.
3. Draw a pixel at each computed point.

Bresenham's algorithm is an efficient integer-only line drawing algorithm that avoids floating-point arithmetic. It uses an error term to decide when to increment the secondary coordinate.

**Drawing a rectangle:**

A rectangle is drawn by drawing four lines (top, bottom, left, right) or by filling the rectangle with a color.

**Drawing a circle (Midpoint circle algorithm):**

The circle drawing algorithm uses symmetry to draw a circle by computing points in one octant and mirroring them to the other seven octants. The algorithm uses the equation `x^2 + y^2 = r^2` and increments x while adjusting y based on the error term.

**Output module:**

The Output module provides text output on the screen. It maintains a cursor position (row, column) and prints characters at that position. The screen has 23 rows of text (each text row is 11 pixels high) and 64 columns (each character is 8 pixels wide).

The Output module stores a font: a bitmap for each character (ASCII 32 to 126). Each character is an 11×8 bitmap. When printing a character, the Output module copies the character's bitmap to the screen at the current cursor position.

**Character set:**

The Jack OS font includes all printable ASCII characters. Each character is stored as an array of 11 integers, each integer representing one row of 8 pixels. The font is stored in the Output module's static data.

**Cursor management:**

The Output module maintains the cursor position (current row and column). When printing a character, it advances the cursor. When reaching the end of a row, it moves to the next row. When reaching the end of the screen, it may scroll or wrap.

screens.title: Screen Graphics and Output
screens.subtitle: Pixels, lines, shapes, and text on the Hack screen

narration.text: In this lesson we’ll explore the Screen and Output modules of the Jack operating system and why they matter. You will learn how the Hack screen is laid out in memory, how to set individual pixels, and how integer-only algorithms draw lines and circles efficiently. We’ll also see how text is produced by copying small bitmap fonts to the screen and how the cursor tracks text placement. These topics are foundational: they translate low-level memory addresses into visible pixels and readable text, and they reveal how clever algorithms compensate for hardware limits. For example, Bresenham’s line algorithm avoids floating-point math so the Hack C P U can draw straight lines fast. A second concrete benefit is that bitmap fonts let the Output module render characters with simple memory copies, which is essential on minimal hardware. By the end you’ll be ready to implement drawPixel, drawLine, drawRectangle, drawCircle, and simple text printing routines. Think about one question as we go: how does an array of words become a house, a checkerboard, and a typed message on the screen?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Screen and Output map memory to pixels and characters so software can paint graphics and typeset text efficiently on the Hack platform.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will implement the Screen and Output modules and use them to produce simple graphics and text programs. First, you will be able to compute the address and bit position for any pixel on the Hack screen and explain why the screen uses words of 16 bits. Second, you will understand and code drawing primitives: a function to set a pixel, an integer-only line algorithm, rectangle drawing and circle drawing using symmetry. Third, you will implement the Output module that holds a bitmap font and a cursor; you will print characters and strings by copying bitmaps to the appropriate screen addresses. Finally, you will test your modules with small programs such as a checkerboard, a rendered house, and printing numbers. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: address math, integer algorithms that match hardware constraints, and simple bitmap rendering. These skills show how low-level memory access becomes a visible image and provide a solid foundation for more advanced graphics work.

narration.text: These objectives build practical systems skills. Computing pixel addresses teaches pointer arithmetic and bit masking — essential low-level programming techniques. Implementing Bresenham and the midpoint circle algorithm trains you to convert mathematical geometry into integer steps that hardware can execute quickly. Building an Output module with a bitmap font shows how high-level abstractions — characters and cursor movement — rest on small, fixed-size memory copies. Practically, these skills let you write simple GUIs, games, and text consoles on minimal hardware. In the Hack ecosystem they are also testable: small unit tests can verify pixel addresses, and visual programs like a checkerboard or a drawn house give concrete feedback. Finally, knowing when to use a bitmap font versus a more complex approach is a trade-off lesson about memory, speed, and size. Ask yourself: which trade-off would you take for a tiny handheld device?

screens.title: Screen memory map
screens.subtitle: How rows, words, and bits form the 256×512 pixel canvas

narration.text: The Hack screen is a tightly packed memory image. Conceptually it is 256 rows high and 512 pixels wide where every pixel is either black or white. The hardware exposes that canvas as a block of memory starting at address sixteen thousand three hundred eighty-four and extending to twenty-four thousand five hundred seventy-five. Each row contains 512 pixels. Those 512 pixels are stored as thirty-two 16-bit words because 32 times 16 equals 512. This layout matters because to change a single pixel you compute which row you are on, which 16-bit word inside that row holds the pixel, and which bit inside the word corresponds to the column. The address formula you will use is address = 16384 + row * 32 + wordIndex. The bit position inside the word is the column modulo 16. A quick concrete example: pixel at column 30 on row 10 lives in word index 30 divided by 16 equals 1, and bit position 30 modulo 16 equals 14. Understanding this mapping is the essential first step before you implement any drawing primitive because efficient set and clear operations depend on correct address and mask calculation.

keyIdea.title: Memory mapping rule
keyIdea.text: Pixel address = 16384 + row * 32 + (col / 16); bit = col % 16. Rows × 32 words × 16 bits = 256 × 512 pixels.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Screen memory map
Definition

256 rows × 512 columns

The screen memory block is contiguous. Each row is stored as thirty-two 16-bit words. Use the address formula to locate any pixel's word.

Address formulas
Word address: 16384 + row * 32 + wordIndex
Bit position: col % 16
Key Takeaway

Correct pixel addressing avoids drawing corruption and is the basis for all other primitives.

Annotated example
Example: pixel (col=30, row=10)
wordIndex = 30 / 16 = 1, bit = 30 % 16 = 14
// compute word address for (30,10)
address = 16384 + 10 * 32 + 1
// mask for bit 14: 1 << 14
Visual mnemonic
Think of each row as a shelf holding 32 boxes; each box contains 16 paint dots. Choose the shelf, box, then dot index.
Common mistake
Off-by-one errors in dividing columns by 16 or incorrect modulo operations often place the mask in the wrong word. Always test with several columns including multiples of 16.

narration.text: Drawing a single pixel requires three concrete operations: compute the correct word address, build a mask for the bit inside that word, and perform a read-modify-write to set or clear the bit. First compute the word index as the column divided by sixteen, and the bit position as column modulo sixteen. Then compute the address by adding the base screen address with row times thirty-two plus the word index. To turn a pixel black you OR the current word with the mask; to make it white you AND with the inverse of the mask. The read before write preserves neighbor pixels in the same word. A typical implementation uses integer shifts for the mask: one shifted left by the bit position. A concrete example helps: for (x=30,y=10) the mask is one shifted left by fourteen. Common mistakes include forgetting to cast division to integer semantics or accidentally shifting by the full column rather than the modulo result. Always test setting a pixel, clearing it, then toggling it to ensure the whole sequence works. This small routine is the building block for lines, rectangles, circles, and text rendering.

keyIdea.title: Implement drawPixel
keyIdea.text: Compute address = 16384 + y * 32 + x / 16; mask = 1 << (x % 16); read word, combine with mask, write back.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Drawing a single pixel
Goal
Set or clear one pixel without disturbing neighboring pixels in the same word.
Step-by-step
  1. wordIndex = x / 16; bit = x % 16
  2. address = 16384 + y * 32 + wordIndex
  3. mask = 1 << bit
  4. value = read(address); write(address, value | mask) to set, or value & ~mask to clear
Common mistake

Using column instead of column modulo 16 when shifting will overflow the mask and affect wrong bits.

Code example (Jack-style pseudocode)
// drawPixel(x, y)
wordIndex = x / 16
bit = x % 16
addr = 16384 + y * 32 + wordIndex
mask = 1 << bit
value = Memory[addr]
// set pixel to black
Memory[addr] = value | mask
// to clear pixel: Memory[addr] = value & ~mask
Analogy
Think of each 16-bit word as a row of 16 lamps; you switch one lamp without resetting the rest by using a stencil (mask).

screens.title: Drawing lines with Bresenham
screens.subtitle: Integer-only line drawing using an error term

narration.text: Drawing a straight line from one point to another on a pixel grid requires deciding which pixels best approximate the mathematical line. Bresenham’s algorithm does this using only integer arithmetic. Start by computing dx and dy as the coordinate differences. Decide whether to iterate along x or along y based on which difference is larger; this keeps the main loop incrementing the dominant coordinate. Maintain an error term that accumulates the discrepancy between the ideal line and the chosen discrete points. At each step increment the dominant coordinate by one and add the smaller difference to the error term. When the error crosses a threshold, increment the secondary coordinate and subtract the scaled threshold from the error. For example, drawing a line from (2,3) to (10,7) uses dx = 8 and dy = 4; you step x each loop and occasionally increment y. The big advantage on Hack is that everything is addition, subtraction, and bit shifts — no division or floating point. A common misconception is that Bresenham is complex; in practice it reduces to a few integer adds and a conditional per pixel. Implement it by calling drawPixel at every loop iteration, and test with horizontal, vertical, diagonal, and steep lines to be confident.

keyIdea.title: Bresenham's insight
keyIdea.text: Use an integer error accumulator to choose when to step the secondary coordinate, avoiding floating-point arithmetic entirely.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Drawing lines with Bresenham
Algorithm overview
Compute dx, dy, choose major axis, and iterate while maintaining an integer error term to know when to step the minor axis.
Steps
  1. dx = abs(x2 - x1), dy = abs(y2 - y1)
  2. Decide if line is steep: if dy > dx swap axes
  3. Set error = 2*dy - dx (scaled integer accumulator)
  4. For i from 0 to dx: plot pixel; error += 2*dy; if error > 0 then y += step; error -= 2*dx
Check your understanding
Why is axis-swapping used for steep lines? Think about which coordinate should be incremented each loop to keep the loop count low and arithmetic simple.
Concrete example
Line from (2,3) to (10,7)
dx=8, dy=4; iterate 8 steps across x, increment y on error threshold crossings. Call drawPixel at each computed (x,y).
Common misconception
Bresenham isn’t about approximating lines poorly — it chooses the best pixel each step using simple integer arithmetic, yielding visually straight lines at low cost.
Pro tip

Test with steep and shallow slopes to validate axis swapping and sign handling for negative slopes.

screens.title: Rectangles and filling strategies
screens.subtitle: Outline vs filled rectangles using lines and scans

narration.text: Rectangles are built from lines or by filling spans. A rectangle’s outline can be drawn with four calls to a line routine: top, bottom, left, and right. This is straightforward and economical if you only need the border. Filling a rectangle efficiently often uses horizontal scanlines: for each y between top and bottom compute the left and right x bounds and set contiguous pixels by manipulating whole words when possible. On the Hack platform, where a word contains sixteen pixels, fill routines should align to word boundaries when possible and use full-word writes rather than per-pixel operations to improve speed. Practically, you compute leftWord and rightWord for a scanline; set partial masks for the edge words and fill full words by writing 0xFFFF. A common trade-off is code complexity versus speed: a simple nested loop that calls drawPixel for every position is easy to write and correct but will be much slower than a word-aligned fill. Test with both methods: for small rectangles the overhead of alignment may not matter, but for large fills the word-oriented method is substantially faster.

keyIdea.title: Rectangle strategy
keyIdea.text: Use line primitives for borders and word-aligned scanline fills for fast filled rectangles; prefer full-word writes when possible.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Rectangles and filling strategies
Outline vs filled
Outlines: four lines. Filled: scanlines that write masks and full words where possible for speed.
Scanline fill pattern
  1. For each row y between y1 and y2 compute leftX and rightX.
  2. leftWord = leftX / 16, rightWord = rightX / 16
  3. Write partial masks to edge words; write 0xFFFF to full words between them.
Example
Fill rectangle from x=10 to x=70 on row y: leftWord=0, rightWord=4, set masks for word 0 and 4, write full words for 1..3.
Performance note
Per-pixel loops are simpler but slow. Word-level writes reduce memory operations and are recommended for large fills on Hack.
Common mistake
Ignoring word alignment causes excessive read-modify-write calls and can produce visual seams on edges. Plan edge masks explicitly.
Try this
Implement both pixel-by-pixel and word-aligned fills and compare execution speed for large rectangles.

screens.title: Midpoint circle algorithm
screens.subtitle: Draw circles using symmetry and an integer error term

narration.text: Drawing a circle on a discrete pixel grid uses symmetry to minimize computation. The midpoint circle algorithm computes points for one octant and mirrors them into the remaining seven. Start with x = 0 and y = radius. Maintain a decision parameter that determines when to decrement y as x increments. The decision parameter tracks the midpoint between candidate pixels; when the parameter becomes negative you move horizontally, otherwise you move diagonally and adjust the parameter accordingly. The heavy lifting is done by integer addition and subtraction. Each computed (x,y) in the first octant produces eight symmetric points: (x,y), (y,x), and the reflected variants across axes and sign flips. A concrete example: for r = 5 start with (0,5); plot symmetric points for each incremental x until x > y. Common misconceptions include forgetting to mirror signs correctly, which produces incomplete circles, or using floating point radii which complicate integer steps. Implement the octant loop and a small helper that plots all eight mirror points using drawPixel; this yields a visually round shape with minimal arithmetic suited to the Hack platform.

keyIdea.title: Circle drawing insight
keyIdea.text: Compute one octant with integer updates and mirror points to draw the full circle efficiently.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Midpoint circle algorithm
Core idea
Use integer decision variable and symmetry of circle octants to reduce computation.
Octant mirroring
Each (x,y) in the first octant yields eight pixels across reflections and swaps: mirror across axes and swap x/y.
Step loop
  1. Initialize x=0, y=r, d=1-r (decision variable)
  2. Plot eight mirrors of (x,y)
  3. Increment x; if d < 0 then d += 2*x + 1 else y-- and d += 2*(x - y) + 1
  4. Repeat until x > y
Concrete example
r = 5: start (0,5). Plot all eight symmetric pixels for each computed pair until x passes y, producing a closed, symmetric circle of pixels.
Common mistake
Plotting only one octant without mirroring yields an eighth of the circle. Remember sign swaps and axis swaps for full coverage.
Try this
Implement midpoint loop and draw circles of varying radii to check symmetry visually.

screens.title: Output module and bitmap fonts
screens.subtitle: How text is rendered as 11×8 bitmaps

narration.text: The Output module renders text by copying fixed-size bitmaps for each printable character into the screen memory. The font used in Jack is a bitmap font where each character occupies eleven rows and eight columns of pixels. Each character is stored as an array of eleven integers; each integer encodes eight bits representing a row of the glyph. When the Output module prints a character, it takes the glyph’s eleven integers and writes their bits to the corresponding screen addresses starting at the cursor’s pixel coordinate. This approach is simple and very fast on hardware like Hack because rendering becomes memory copies and bit operations rather than geometry. A concrete sequence: locate the cursor’s row and column in pixel coordinates, compute the word and bit offsets for each of the eleven rows of the glyph, then copy bits into the screen words using masks. The trade-offs are clear: bitmap fonts are fast and straightforward but fixed-size; they cannot scale smoothly. For the Hack platform, the reduction in computation and code size outweighs the lack of scalability. Output module and bitmap fonts means characters are 11×8 bitmaps stored as arrays of integers; printing copies these rows into screen memory at the cursor position.. In practical terms, how text is rendered as 11×8 bitmaps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bitmap font rule
keyIdea.text: Characters are 11×8 bitmaps stored as arrays of integers; printing copies these rows into screen memory at the cursor position.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Output module and bitmap fonts
Key facts
  • Each character is 11 rows × 8 columns of pixels.
  • Characters are stored as arrays of 11 integers (one per row).
  • Printing copies these rows into the screen at the cursor position.
Rendering steps
For each glyph row compute the destination word addresses and masks and write bits using read-modify-write or aligned full-word writes when possible.
Analogy
Think of each character as a rubber stamp with 11 horizontal stripes; stamping copies the black dots into the canvas row by row.
Concrete example
// glyph for 'A' stored as 11 integers
glyphA = [0x18,0x24,0x24,0x24,0x3C,0x24,0x24,0x24,0x24,0x00,0x00]
// copy each integer row into the screen at cursor position
Common trade-off
Bitmap fonts are memory-specific and fixed size. They are fast but cannot be scaled without new bitmaps for each size.

screens.title: Cursor management and printing utilities
screens.subtitle: Rows, columns, scrolling, and printing primitives

narration.text: The Output module keeps track of a cursor in text coordinates and uses it to place characters on the screen. The screen supports twenty-three text rows because each character is eleven pixels tall and the available height divides into those rows; each character is eight pixels wide and there are sixty-four columns across. When printing a character the Output module copies its bitmap at the current cursor pixel coordinates then advances the cursor column. When the cursor reaches the end of a text row it moves to the next row and may scroll the screen if necessary. Printing a string iterates over characters and calls the printChar helper for each glyph. Printing an integer usually converts the integer to a string and then prints the characters. The println operation advances the cursor to the start of the next line. Important implementation details include handling carriage returns, clipping glyphs at screen edges, and implementing scrolling by copying screen memory upward and clearing the last lines. A common pitfall is failing to convert between text coordinates and pixel coordinates correctly; always multiply text row by eleven and text column by eight when computing pixel offsets.

keyIdea.title: Cursor rule
keyIdea.text: Cursor position uses text rows and columns; pixel offset = row * 11, column * 8. PrintChar copies glyph then advances cursor, handling wrap and scroll.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Cursor management and printing utilities
Text geometry
23 text rows (11 px tall) × 64 columns (8 px wide). Cursor tracks row and column; pixel offset = row*11, col*8.
Printing helpers
  • printChar(c): copy glyph at cursor, advance cursor
  • printString(s): iterate characters and call printChar
  • printInt(i): convert integer to characters then print
  • println(): move cursor to next line, possibly scroll
Edge cases
Clipping glyphs at screen edges and implementing smooth scrolling are common implementation details you must handle for a robust Output module.
Concrete example
To print '42' convert 42 to the characters '4' and '2', call printChar for each, and ensure the cursor advances correctly between characters and lines.
Common pitfall
Mixing pixel and text coordinates leads to misaligned text. Always convert using the 11×8 character cell size before writing bitmaps.

screens.title: Implementing and testing primitives
screens.subtitle: A guided sequence: pixel → line → rectangle → circle → text

narration.text: A practical implementation path reduces bugs and provides testable milestones. Start with drawPixel and unit-test by setting and clearing individual pixels at different columns, including boundaries at multiples of sixteen. Next implement drawLine using Bresenham and test horizontal, vertical, diagonal, and steep lines. After lines are reliable, build rectangle functions: first drawRectangle that calls drawLine for borders, then implement a fast fill that uses scanline word writes. Implement drawCircle using the midpoint algorithm and mirror octants; verify symmetry by drawing concentric circles. Finally implement the Output module: load or define an eleven-by-eight bitmap for a few ASCII characters, write printChar to copy the glyph to the cursor pixel position, and add printString and println utilities. Test the full pipeline by writing small programs: draw a checkerboard using alternating filled rectangles, draw a house by combining rectangles and triangles, and print text labels on the scene. Each test gives visual feedback; if pixels misalign revisit the address math. This incremental approach helps isolate errors and gives fast visual verification. Implementing and testing primitives means build and test in stages: drawpixel → drawline → drawrectangle/fill → drawcircle → output.printchar and string utilities.. In practical terms, a guided sequence: pixel → line → rectangle → circle → text. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implementation path
keyIdea.text: Build and test in stages: drawPixel → drawLine → drawRectangle/fill → drawCircle → Output.printChar and string utilities.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Implementing and testing primitives
Step sequence
  1. Implement drawPixel and test boundary pixels.
  2. Add Bresenham drawLine and test common slopes.
  3. Create rectangle routines and test filled vs outline.
  4. Implement midpoint circle and test symmetry.
  5. Build Output module and print sample strings.
Example test
Draw a checkerboard of 8×8 tiles using filled rectangles and then print a label. If the label aligns with tiles, pixel math is correct.
Scenario: draw a house
Use a filled rectangle for the body, a triangle made from three lines for the roof, and print a title below. Visual inspection makes it easy to detect off-by-one addressing bugs.
Common debugging tips
Log computed addresses for a few pixels, test multiples of 16, and simplify tests to single-row draws to isolate masking errors.

screens.title: Algorithm trade-offs and assessment
screens.subtitle: Why Bresenham and bitmaps suit Hack; compare naive approaches

narration.text: When designing drawing routines for the Hack platform we must consider both algorithmic cost and hardware capabilities. Bresenham’s algorithm is integer-only, using additions, subtractions, and conditionals. The naive approach — calculating each pixel’s ideal coordinate using floating-point slopes and rounding — would require floating-point arithmetic or emulation on Hack, which is both slow and complex. The Hack C P U performs integer operations quickly; therefore Bresenham matches the available instruction set and memory bandwidth. For fonts, bitmap glyphs are cheap to render because printing is a set of memory copies and bitwise masks. A vector font would require generating curves and rasterizing them, which is computationally expensive and memory-hungry. The trade-offs are: bitmaps are fixed-size but fast and simple, vectors are scalable but expensive to render. For the Hack environment the minimalist, memory-oriented choices are correct. An assessment question to solidify this: explain why integer-only algorithms are essential on Hack and outline the performance and implementation costs of a floating-point alternative. Algorithm trade-offs and assessment means bresenham and bitmap fonts trade generality for speed and simplicity, matching the hack computer's integer-only, low-memory environment.. In practical terms, why bresenham and bitmaps suit hack; compare naive approaches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: Bresenham and bitmap fonts trade generality for speed and simplicity, matching the Hack computer's integer-only, low-memory environment.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Algorithm trade-offs and assessment
Compare
Integer-only algorithms vs naive floating-point approaches; bitmap fonts vs vector rendering.
Why integers win on Hack
Hack lacks floating-point hardware. Integer algorithms avoid software-emulated floats and keep code and runtime smaller and faster.
Font trade-offs
Bitmap: fast, simple, fixed-size. Vector: scalable but requires complex rasterization and more CPU time.
Assessment idea
Describe why Bresenham’s integer-only steps are essential on Hack and compare the runtime cost of a floating-point naive line algorithm versus Bresenham.
Misconception
Assuming floating-point algorithms are required for quality. On pixel grids, integer algorithms give precise, efficient results.

narration.text: Here are the key concepts to hold onto. First, the screen memory map translates rows and columns into addresses and bit positions: address equals base plus row times thirty-two plus the word index, and bit equals column modulo sixteen. Second, drawPixel is a read-modify-write using a mask computed with a shift; this preserves neighboring pixels in the same word. Third, Bresenham and the midpoint circle algorithm use integer accumulators and symmetry to draw lines and circles without floating point, which is crucial on the Hack C P U. Fourth, the Output module renders text by copying 11×8 bitmap glyphs to the screen and advancing a cursor in text coordinates. Finally, practical implementations balance simplicity and speed: per-pixel loops are easy to write, while word-aligned fills and full-word writes yield higher performance. Keep these rules in mind when building and testing your modules.

keyIdea.title: Memorize
keyIdea.text: Address math, mask construction, integer algorithms, and bitmap text are the core building blocks of screen output on Hack.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Key Concepts
Screen memory map
256×512 pixels as 32 words per row starting at address 16384.
Bresenham & circles
Integer-only line algorithm and midpoint circle using symmetry.
Bitmap text
Characters are 11×8 bitmaps copied to the screen; cursor manages placement.
Takeaway

Practical graphics on constrained hardware rely on careful memory layout and integer algorithms; these building blocks let you draw shapes and render text efficiently.

narration.text: As you finish this lesson, keep three compact ideas at hand. Second, use integer algorithms like Bresenham and the midpoint circle to draw accurate shapes with only additions, subtractions, and bit shifts. Third, text output is simply bitmap stamping: each character is an eleven-by-eight grid copied into screen memory and advanced by a cursor that translates text coordinates into pixel offsets.
